pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 6-7 (Y2), CONCEPTUAL. Understand and APPLY the commutative property of addition: addends can be added in any order (3+8 = 8+3), and recognise that subtraction is NOT commutative (5−3 ≠ 3−5). A central property node (0.16) — it halves the facts to learn and licenses 'put the bigger number first' to count on.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y2): 'show that addition of 2 numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of 1 number from another cannot'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 1.OA.3 'apply properties of operations as strategies to add and subtract… (Commutative property of addition)'.
• Operational details — Show commutativity structurally, not as a rule to memorise: the SAME set of objects seen two ways (a rod of 3 and a rod of 8 make the same length however ordered; a part-whole with parts swapped gives the same whole). Then exploit it strategically — to add 3+8, start from 8 and count on 3. Deliberately CONTRAST subtraction (take 3 from 5 vs 5 from 3) to show order matters there, preventing over-generalisation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 6): show 3+8 and 8+3 give the same total with objects. Tier B (age 6-7): use commutativity to count on from the larger addend. Tier C (age 7): explain why addition is commutative but subtraction is not, with an example.
bestPractices: Demonstrate commutativity with a model that is literally unchanged by reordering — the same two rods/bars, the same part-whole with parts swapped — so it's seen as structural, not a memorised rule.
Immediately put it to work: 'start with the bigger number and count on', showing the property makes calculation easier.
Explicitly contrast subtraction (5−3 vs 3−5) so children learn the property is specific to addition and don't over-generalise 'you can swap them'.
Use it to reduce fact load — knowing 3+8 gives 8+3 — linking to fluency work.
Have children justify with a drawing or rearrangement rather than just asserting the rule.
keyRepresentations: Two number rods/bars combined, then physically swapped (same total length)
Part-part-whole model with the two parts swapped
A rotated array/ten-frame showing the same quantity two ways
Empty number line: 8 then +3 vs 3 then +8 landing on the same point
Contrast pair for subtraction (5−3 and 3−5) showing different results
commonMisconceptions: Over-generalising to subtraction (thinking 5−3 = 3−5) — the key error this topic must pre-empt.
Treating a+b and b+a as different facts to learn separately.
Believing the answer changes with order because the counting process feels different.
Applying 'swap them' to word problems where order encodes meaning (start/change).
Not using commutativity strategically (counting on from the smaller number, doing more work).

learn.summary: For ages 6-7, teach the commutative property of addition structurally: the same two amounts combine to the same whole whichever order they are taken (3+8 = 8+3), then exploit this to count on from the larger addend. Deliberately contrast subtraction (5−3 ≠ 3−5) so children do not over-generalise 'you can swap them'. The core insight is invariance (the addition total holds under reordering) versus change (the subtraction result shifts), and children should justify why, not just recite a rule.

activities.title: Swap bench: watch the addition total hold
feedback: If the child expects the total to change after swapping: rebuild both orders on the SAME set of objects so there is visibly one unchanging quantity combined two ways.
If the child says 5−3 and 3−5 are the same: show that 3 cannot have 5 removed (you run out), while 5−3 = 2 can be done — so order is load-bearing for take-away.
Reinforce by asking them to predict the swapped total before revealing it, then confirm it matches.
activities.rationale: A model that is literally unchanged by reordering (same rods, same part-whole) lets children see commutativity as structural rather than a memorised rule, and contrasting subtraction in the same model targets the main over-generalisation error.
sourceClaims: Y2 pupils show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction cannot.
Commutativity is best shown structurally (same quantity rearranged) and contrasted with non-commutative subtraction to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Combine two bars or rods — one of 3 and one of 8 — into a single total bar, and note the total (11).
Swap the two parts so 8 comes first and 3 second, and check whether the total bar's length changes.
On a number line, trace 8 then count on 3, and separately 3 then count on 8, and mark where each lands.
Say aloud what stayed the same and what moved: the parts traded places but the whole did not change.
Switch to subtraction: build 5 then remove 3, then try 3 then remove 5, and describe what happens when you try to take 5 from 3.
activities.intendedInsight: Reordering the two addends rearranges the parts but leaves the whole unchanged, so a+b = b+a; subtraction starts from one amount and removes the other, so swapping changes what you begin with and the result changes.

activities.title: Count on from the bigger number
feedback: If the child recounts from scratch instead of reusing the known fact: build both orders on the same counters to show it is one unchanging total, then practise stating the swapped fact immediately.
If the child counts on from the smaller number: compare how many steps each order takes to make the efficiency visible.
activities.rationale: Putting the property to work shows it reduces fact load and makes calculation easier, linking commutativity to fluency rather than leaving it as an abstract statement.
sourceClaims: 1.OA.3: apply properties of operations as strategies, including the commutative property of addition.
learnerActions: Given 3+8, decide which number to start from so there is less counting on to do, and explain your choice.
Count on from the larger addend to reach the total, then check against counting on from the smaller to confirm they agree.
Try 2+9: say which order you would count on from and why.
State the matching fact instantly: if you know 8+3, say 3+8 without recounting.
activities.intendedInsight: Because order does not change an addition total, you can always start from the larger number and count on the smaller one, which takes fewer steps (unless the two numbers are equal, as in 6+6) — commutativity is a calculation-saving strategy, and knowing one fact gives you its partner.

activities.title: Convince me: why addition swaps but subtraction doesn't
feedback: If the child claims 8−5 = 5−8: have them physically attempt to take 8 from a pile of 5 — it cannot be done — and name addition as the only one of the two that is commutative.
If the justification is 'because that's the rule': ask for a drawing or counter arrangement that shows the whole staying the same.
activities.rationale: The objective includes justifying why addition commutes but subtraction does not; prompting the child to explain and to test the claim on subtraction develops that reasoning directly through the structural contrast.
sourceClaims: Commutativity is best shown structurally (same quantity rearranged) and contrasted with non-commutative subtraction to prevent over-generalisation.
learnerActions: Argue why 3+8 must equal 8+3, using a drawing or a rearrangement of objects rather than just asserting the rule.
Test whether the same swap works for take-away: predict, then model 8−5 and 5−8 with counters and report what happens.
Consider 6+6: does order matter here, and what does that tell you about the rule?
State in your own words which operation can be reordered and why the other cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition combines the same two amounts whichever order you take them, so the whole is unchanged; subtraction removes one amount from another, so swapping changes the starting amount and the result. Justifying this builds reasoning beyond recall.

activities.title: True/false and matching checks
feedback: If a subtraction pair is marked true: return to counters to show the results differ (5−3 = 2, but with 3 counters you run out and cannot take 5 away).
If the child cannot pick the efficient order: compare the number of count-on steps for each option.
activities.rationale: True/false, matching and strategy-choice items assess the property and the non-commutativity of subtraction. These recognition items check understanding but do not on their own elicit the child rearranging quantities or justifying; pair them with the swap and justification activities.
learnerActions: Decide whether statements are true or false: is 3+8 = 8+3? is 5−3 = 3−5?
Match each addition to its swapped partner that gives the same total.
Choose which order is easier to count on from for a given sum, and say why.
activities.intendedInsight: Addition statements hold when the order is swapped; subtraction statements do not. Recognising this consolidates the distinction and the strategic use of counting on from the larger number.

constraints: Show commutativity structurally — the same quantity rearranged — not as a rule to memorise.
Always include the subtraction contrast (e.g. 5−3 vs 3−5); omitting it risks children over-generalising 'you can swap them'.
Watch for word-problem contexts where order encodes meaning (start/change); 'swap them' should not be applied there.

Recognition-only items (true/false, matching, multiple choice) assess understanding but do not by themselves elicit the child independently rearranging quantities or justifying; use them alongside construction and explanation tasks.

A static side-by-side of 3+8 and 8+3 with the same objects can anchor the property, but it does not let the child perform the swap and watch the total hold; treat it as a scaffold toward hands-on or responsive work.
When demonstrating 5−8 or 3−5 with young children, frame it as 'you run out / cannot take that many away' rather than introducing negative numbers as a target concept.
When contrasting a subtraction pair, keep the two numbers consistent across the action and its feedback (e.g. 5−3 vs 3−5), so the 'you run out' example matches the pair the child is working with.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original labelled a live invariance-vs-change contrast as 'impossible statically' and said 3D 'adds nothing'; these are catalog-fit claims, not established necessity. They have been softened to scoped affordances (a static image cannot be manipulated but can still anchor the property).

Of the three cited sources, two are marked unverified in the source row (CCSS-M 1.OA.3 and the NCETM mastery claim); only the DfE National Curriculum claim is marked verified. Treat citation strength accordingly.

The assessment's probe '5 − 8' and 'take 5 cubes and try to remove 8' edges toward negative numbers; for ages 6-7 this is best handled as 'cannot be done / goes below what you have' rather than teaching negatives, which has been reflected in the constraints.

Independent re-audit confirmed Activity 1's subtraction feedback now matches its stated 5−3/3−5 pair ('3 cannot have 5 removed'), Activity 3 consistently uses the 8−5/5−8 pair, and all arithmetic (3+8=8+3=11, 2+9, 5−3=2, 8−5=3) is correct; no remaining internal contradictions or unsupported categorical modality claims were found.

assess.poeTask: Predict whether 5 − 8 gives the same answer as 8 − 5. Say your prediction and WHY first. Then take 8 cubes and remove 5, and take 5 cubes and try to remove 8. What happened, and what does it tell you about doing subtraction 'in any order'?
probeDeeper: Why does swapping the two numbers not change the total in an addition?
You said 8 − 5 isn't the same as 5 − 8 — show me with counters why not.
What about 6 + 6 — does order matter there? What does that tell you about the rule?
For 2 + 9, which order would you choose to count on from, and why?
assess.correctAnswer: 5 + 8 = 13 (the same, because order doesn't change an addition). But 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 are NOT the same: 8 − 5 = 3, while 5 − 8 cannot be done with these counters / goes below zero. Reason: addition combines the same two amounts whichever order you take them; subtraction starts from one amount and removes the other, so swapping changes what you begin with.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'You can do any sum in any order' — over-applies commutativity to subtraction, claiming 5 − 8 = 8 − 5 = 3.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model 8−5 and 5−8 with counters — you cannot take 8 from a pile of 5; order matters. Name addition as the only one of the two that is commutative.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: asserts subtraction gives the same answer whichever way round.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'I'd better count it again' — does not trust that swapping preserves the total, so recomputes 5 + 8 from one instead of using the known fact.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show both orders built on the SAME set of counters or the same bar; the total is one unchanging quantity. Practise stating the swapped fact instantly.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Counts all / counts on from scratch rather than stating 13 immediately.

responseLevels.gap: Recomputes both additions and/or thinks order changes an addition total, or claims subtraction is commutative.
responseLevels.full: States the addition total is unchanged because the same amounts are combined, uses commutativity to count on from the larger addend, AND correctly denies that subtraction is commutative, justifying with counters.
responseLevels.partial: Knows addition works in any order and uses it to count on from the larger, but over-generalises to subtraction OR cannot explain why the total is unchanged.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: I know that 8 + 5 = 13. So what is 5 + 8? And does the same trick work for taking away — do 8 − 5 and 5 − 8 give the same answer? Tell me why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child running a shallow 'any order works' rule gives the addition right AND wrongly says 8−5 = 5−8; a child who understands commutativity as 'the same quantities combined' restricts it to addition and rejects it for subtraction. The addition half is easy for everyone — the subtraction contrast is what separates real understanding from an over-applied slogan.
